At Coos, he received Ptolemy the captain, who had defected from Antigonus, but later imprisoned and poisoned him with hemlock; he incorporated the captain's soldiers into his own army.

l: Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: He raised a large army and restored Hercules, Alexander's son by Bargine, to his father's kingdom. Cassander's promises persuaded him to join a secret agreement to murder Hercules, after which he openly joined Cassander, received troops, and later withdrew into Locris after being opposed in Boeotia and Peloponnesus.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Polyperchon restored him, as the son of Alexander, to his father's kingdom. Cassander feared that the Macedonians would support him and persuaded Polyperchon to have him murdered.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: He opposed the restoration of Hercules because he feared that the Macedonians would revolt to him. He persuaded Polyperchon to murder Hercules by promising him honors, commands, troops, and a share in the principality.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: As general of the Carthaginian forces in Sicily, he reduced much of the island and besieged Syracuse by cutting off its supplies. The Syracusans defeated his army at night, captured him, and delivered him to people who tortured and killed him; his head was then sent to Agathocles.

l: Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: He received Amilcar's head in Africa and used it to show the Carthaginians that their forces in Sicily had been destroyed. After his son Archagathus caused a mutiny by killing Lyciscus, Agathocles risked death, regained the soldiers' loyalty through a speech and apparent attempt at suicide, and then defeated the Carthaginians in a sudden attack.

l: Archagathus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: He became enraged when Lyciscus insulted him and accused him of an incestuous relationship with his stepmother, Alcia. Archagathus seized a lance and killed Lyciscus, provoking a mutiny in which the soldiers threatened to kill him and Agathocles.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Its political situation became unstable after the defeat of the Carthaginian army at Syracuse. The Agrigentines attempted to gain command of the island and encouraged cities to recover their liberty, while Xenodicus freed or attacked several places held by the Carthaginians.

l: Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Agathocles was operating there when he received Amilcar's head and displayed it to the Carthaginians. His successes were followed by a dangerous mutiny among his own soldiers.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Cassander feared that its naturally inconstant people would revolt in favor of Hercules. After Hercules was murdered, Polyperchon openly joined Cassander and was advanced in Macedonia.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: It was besieged by Amilcar, who cut off provisions and destroyed the surrounding crops. Its defenders seized the fort at Euryclus, defeated the Carthaginians in a nighttime engagement, captured Amilcar, and later suffered the loss of ten ships while attempting to obtain grain.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Amilcar was described as one of its noblest citizens and its general in Sicily. After his capture and death, the Carthaginian forces in Sicily lacked a general, and the army divided between its barbarian and Greek elements.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: They besieged Syracuse under Amilcar but were routed at night because of darkness, difficult passages, confusion, and fighting among their own troops. After Amilcar's death, they mourned deeply, became fearful, and later suffered a surprise attack from Agathocles in Africa.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: They anticipated the Carthaginian assault, occupied Euryclus, and defeated Amilcar's army from advantageous ground. They captured Amilcar, tortured and killed him, and later attempted to intercept ships carrying grain to Syracuse.

l: Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: They believed Sicily could be taken after the Carthaginian defeat and created Xenodicus as their general. They captured or liberated several cities, including Gela and Enna, and fought to restore the cities to their ancient laws.

l: the Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: It attacked Syracuse at night with about one hundred and twenty thousand foot and five thousand horse but was thrown into confusion by the terrain, darkness, and disorder among its own men. It was routed, suffered many deaths, and afterward divided between the barbarian and Greek forces.

l: siege of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: Amilcar tried to take Syracuse by cutting off its provisions, destroying the surrounding crops, and occupying the approaches near Olympias. The Syracusans answered with a nighttime sortie that seized Euryclus and led to the defeat and capture of Amilcar.

l: capture of Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: The Syracusans captured Amilcar after routing his army in a nighttime attack near Euryclus. They delivered him to the relatives of those who had been slain, who led him through the city, tortured him, and killed him; his head was sent to Agathocles.

l: Syracusan victory over the Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: A small Syracusan force used an ambush and the advantage of the ground to rout a much larger Carthaginian army. The victory ended the immediate siege of Syracuse, led to the capture of Amilcar, and caused fear and division among the Carthaginians.

l: mutiny of Agathocles's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IL
s: The mutiny began after Archagathus killed Lyciscus, who had insulted him and accused him of adultery with Alcia. The soldiers demanded Archagathus's death, threatened Agathocles if he would not surrender his son, demanded their arrears, and chose new officers; Agathocles regained their allegiance and then defeated the Carthaginians, although more than two hundred mutineers deserted to the enemy.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The account turns to events in Italy, where the Etruscans attacked Sutrium and the Romans divided their forces against the Etruscans and Samnites. Fabius invaded higher Etruria, defeated the Etruscans near Perusia, made peace with several communities, and forced the lifting of the siege of Sutrium, while Marcius took Alifa and relieved the Iapyges. At Rome, the censors Appius Claudius and Caius Plautius undertook major public works and altered the composition of the senate and the organization of citizens, provoking opposition from the nobility. Ptolemy took Andros, Sicyon, and Corinth before returning to Egypt, while Cleopatra was stopped and secretly murdered on Antigonus's orders.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The account next turns to what was done in Italy, including wars involving the Romans, Etruscans, and Samnites.

l: Etruscans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Etruscans attacked Sutrium with a great army and later besieged it. Fabius invaded higher Etruria, defeated them near Perusia, made peace with the Arretines, Crotoneans, and people of Perusia, and forced them to raise the siege of Sutrium.

l: Sutrium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Sutrium, a Roman colony, was attacked and besieged by the Etruscans. The Roman forces defended it, and Fabius eventually forced the Etruscans to withdraw.

l: consuls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The consuls marched with large forces to defend Sutrium and routed the Etruscans. They divided their forces when the Samnites besieged the Iapyges, with Fabius remaining in Etruria and Marcius marching against the Samnites.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Romans defended Sutrium, fought the Etruscans, relieved the Iapyges, and created two censors. They also advanced Caius Flavius, the son of a libertine, to the office of aedile.

l: Samnites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Samnites besieged the Iapyges while the Roman army was far away. Marcius marched against them, took Alifa by storm, and freed the Iapyges from the siege.

l: Iapyges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Iapyges were allies of the Romans and were besieged by the Samnites. Marcius relieved them after taking Alifa.

l: Fabius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Fabius remained in Etruria while the Roman forces were divided, secretly passed through the enemy's bordering country, and raided higher Etruria. He defeated the Etruscans near Perusia, made peace with several communities, took Castula, and forced the lifting of the siege of Sutrium.

l: Etruria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Fabius invaded higher Etruria, a region that had long been free from raids, devastating the countryside, defeating opposing inhabitants, and taking many prisoners.

l: siege of Sutrium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Etruscans besieged Sutrium, but Fabius's victories and capture of Castula forced them to raise the siege.

l: two censors, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Two censors were created at Rome: Appius Claudius and Caius Plautius. They were responsible for taking account of the senators and for the censorial administration described in the account.

l: Appius Claudius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Appius Claudius, serving as censor with Caius Plautius, abrogated many ancient laws, disregarded the senate to gratify the people, brought the Appia water supply into Rome, and constructed much of the Appian Way. He admitted libertines to the senate, allowed citizens to choose their tribes and tax ranks, and supported Caius Flavius's advancement; after leaving office, he kept his house under the pretense of blindness.

l: Roman Senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The senate consented to money being taken from the treasury for Appius Claudius's water project. Appius added libertines to it, which angered the patricians, while the consuls later convened a senate excluding those enrolled by Appius; the people opposed the consuls and supported Appius.

l: Appia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The Appia was a water supply brought into Rome by Appius Claudius from places four furlongs away.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Rome created two censors and received the Appia water supply. Appius Claudius also undertook major road construction extending from Rome to Capua.

l: Appian Way, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The road later called the Appian Way was laid largely with hard stones from Rome to Capua, extending for more than a thousand furlongs. Appius Claudius leveled its rising ground and filled its holes and hollows at great expense.

l: nobility, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: The nobility resented Appius Claudius for disregarding the senate, admitting libertines to it, and promoting people of obscure birth. Appius sought the common people's favor as a defense against their envy.

l: libertines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Libertines were admitted by Appius Claudius into the senate alongside the nobility. Caius Flavius, the son of a libertine, became the first Roman born of a libertine to attain the described honorable office.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Ptolemy sailed from Myndus through the islands to Andros, expelled its garrison, and restored its former liberty. He then received Sicyon and Corinth from Cratesipolis, placed garrisons in them, made peace with Cassander after becoming angry with the Peloponnesians, and returned to Egypt.

l: Sicyon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Sicyon was received by Ptolemy from Cratesipolis. Ptolemy later placed a garrison there before returning to Egypt.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Corinth was received by Ptolemy from Cratesipolis. Ptolemy later placed a garrison there before returning to Egypt.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Cassander made peace with Ptolemy on the condition that each would retain the cities then in his hands.

l: Cleopatra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Having now gone through the affairs of Africa and Sicily, we
s: Cleopatra, angered against Antigonus, went from Sardis toward Ptolemy. Antigonus ordered her to be stopped, and she was later secretly murdered with the help of women; Antigonus had some of those women beheaded and buried Cleopatra magnificently.
